paras: The threatened lynching of Burrell Bland was a threat made in August 1900 against Bland, an elderly Black farmer living near Woodbury, New Jersey, by the family of a white woman he had married in Camden. According to a Camden wire dated August 15, the bride's parents and friends followed the couple and threatened to lynch Bland unless he gave her up. No report of what followed was found, and the marriage itself drew more attention than the threat, appearing as a curiosity in papers from Delaware to the Dakotas.

Bland lived on a small farm near Woodbury, a few miles from Camden. The papers disagreed on the ages of the couple: the wire made him a 71-year-old "negro hermit" and her a 20-year-old Philadelphia girl, while a Camden dispatch of August 16 gave his age as 61 and hers as 31. The bride appears as Eliza Haines in the wire and as Elizabeth Haines elsewhere.

Accounts of how the two met also differ. The wire said she had met him two weeks earlier while tramping across his farm and had visited him nearly every day since, and that her family, learning of the visits, planned to send her away. In a feature from the Philadelphia North American, however, she told the justice that she had loved him since she was a girl, when he worked on her father's farm.

The couple were married at the Camden office of a Black justice of the peace, named as Philip Colling in the wire and P. T. Colding in other reports. The Wilmington Evening Journal placed the ceremony on Tuesday evening, while the wire said it took place on the morning of August 15 after the bride slipped across the river to meet Bland. Once her parents and friends learned of the marriage, the wire reported, they "started on the couple's trail and threatened to lynch the negro if he does not give the girl up."
No report of an attack, an arrest, or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the later stories mentions the family's pursuit.

White papers treated the case as a marriage story rather than a story of violence. The Butler Weekly Times in Missouri ran the wire under "Married Negro Hermit," calling the match the "most astonishing" of several recent marriage "sensations" in Camden and giving the lynching threat as its final sentence without comment. The Evening Journal's short notice, "White Girl Weds Negro," gave only names, ages and the justice, and said nothing of opposition.

A month later the North American feature, "Weds a White Girl," circulated as filler in weeklies in South Dakota, North Dakota and Minnesota between September 20 and 28. It told the story with some sympathy for the couple, closing on the bride's words "I don't care what they say, I love you, Uncle Rell," but it rendered Bland's speech in dialect and described his face as "black as charcoal." No Black-press coverage of the marriage or the threat was found.
The threat rests on the single August 15 wire; the Evening Journal and the North American accounts neither mention nor deny it.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Burrell Bland
bases: The only violence reported is a threat: the bride's parents and friends followed the couple and threatened to lynch Bland unless he gave her up (A2); no attack, capture or injury is reported (A1, A2, A4).
No one was killed or attacked; a single wire report says the white woman's parents and friends threatened to lynch Bland over the interracial marriage (A2), which is a threat, not a lynching.
The marriage is reported independently by three sources (A1, A2, A4), but the pursuit and lynching threat appear only in the Aug. 15 wire (A2); the other accounts neither mention nor deny it.

accounts.label: Camden wire (Aug. 15)
accounts.gist: A 71-year-old 'negro hermit' married a 20-year-old Philadelphia white girl who had met him two weeks before; her family, who had planned to send her away, took the couple's trail and threatened to lynch him if he did not give her up.

accounts.label: Camden dispatch (Aug. 16)
accounts.gist: A 61-year-old colored farmer married a 31-year-old white woman of Camden on Tuesday evening before Justice Colding; no opposition is mentioned.

accounts.label: Philadelphia North American feature
accounts.gist: A scene at Justice Colding's office in which the bride says she had loved Bland since he worked on her father's farm when she was a girl; it mentions no pursuit or threat.

framing.detail: The Missouri reprint headed it 'Married Negro Hermit', called the marriage the 'most astonishing' of Camden's recent 'sensations' and reported the lynching threat without comment.
The Wilmington paper ran a short notice headed 'White Girl Weds Negro' with ages and the justice's name.
The North American feature, 'Weds a White Girl', was sympathetic to the couple's affection but rendered Bland in dialect and described him as having a 'face as black as charcoal'.
